title: Indispensability Arguments in the Philosophy of Mathematics

summaries.example: Imagine scientists making a weather map. The map uses numbers, shapes, and equations to help predict rain. Some philosophers say that if this mathematics is truly needed for the best science, we should take numbers and other mathematical things seriously, not treat them as mere marks on paper. Other philosophers reply that mathematics may be a very useful tool without proving that mathematical objects exist.
summaries.summary: Mathematics is deeply woven into science. It helps scientists make predictions, describe patterns, and state theories clearly. The Quine-Putnam indispensability argument begins with this fact. It says that we should believe in the things that our best scientific theories cannot do without. Since those theories use numbers, sets, functions, and other mathematical ideas, the argument concludes that mathematical objects exist. This conclusion is called mathematical realism, or sometimes platonism. Nominalists disagree. They try to explain how science can use mathematics without believing in mathematical objects. Hartry Field, for example, argues that mathematics might be useful because it makes scientific work simpler, while not adding new physical consequences. Critics also question whether mathematics receives the same evidence as the physical parts of science. A newer version of the argument focuses on explanation: if mathematics genuinely explains why a scientific event happens, perhaps that gives stronger support to realism. The SEP entry presents these arguments and objections without claiming that the debate is settled.
key_ideas: Science uses a great deal of mathematics for predicting, describing, and sometimes explaining what happens.
The Quine-Putnam argument says that we should accept the existence of things that are indispensable to our best scientific theories.
A major disagreement is whether useful mathematics must be true and whether it must show that mathematical objects exist.
Some philosophers argue that mathematics could be replaced by descriptions that mention only physical things.
Another version asks whether mathematics helps explain scientific facts, not merely calculate them.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate asks what our successful scientific theories commit us to believing. It also asks whether usefulness, truth, and explanation are connected. Thinking about it can help us notice the difference between using an idea and believing that the things named by the idea exist. The issue matters to both philosophy of mathematics and philosophy of science.

important_terms.definition: Needed so much for a purpose that removing it would make the result much worse or less useful.
The question of what kinds of things exist.
The view that numbers, sets, and other mathematical objects really exist.
The view that we can talk about mathematics without believing that mathematical objects exist.
The idea that a scientific theory is tested and supported as a whole, including the mathematics it uses.

questions_to_think_about: Can a tool be extremely useful without the things described by the tool really existing?
If a science theory uses numbers, does that give us a reason to believe numbers exist?
Should all parts of a successful theory receive the same support?
Can mathematics explain something, or does it only help us calculate it?

summaries.example: Consider periodical cicadas whose life cycles are 13 or 17 years. One proposed biological explanation is that prime-numbered cycles reduce overlap with predators, competitors, or possible mates whose cycles have other lengths. The explanation uses a fact from number theory: a prime number has no factors other than 1 and itself. Philosophers debate whether the number-theoretic fact genuinely explains the cicadas’ behavior, or whether the real explanation is entirely biological and mathematics merely represents the relevant pattern.
summaries.summary: The SEP entry examines the influential Quine-Putnam indispensability argument for mathematical realism. Its central idea is that ontology—the question of what exists—should follow the commitments of our best scientific theories. The argument’s two main premises are that we should accept all and only indispensable entities in those theories, and that mathematical entities are indispensable. The conclusion is that numbers, sets, functions, and related entities should be accepted as real. The argument’s force depends on several distinctions. Eliminating mathematical language is not enough to show dispensability; the resulting theory must also preserve important scientific virtues. Naturalism supports using science to guide ontology. Confirmational holism is supposed to explain why empirical support for a theory also supports its mathematical components. Critics question both steps. Field argues that mathematics may be conservative—adding no new nominalist consequences—and useful because it simplifies calculation and formulation, rather than because mathematical entities are real. Maddy points to tensions between holism and the actual attitudes and practices of scientists and mathematicians. Sober argues that mathematics may not be tested through empirical competition in the same way as ordinary scientific hypotheses. Explanatory versions of the argument respond by asking whether mathematics contributes genuinely to scientific explanations. The periodic-cicada case is a prominent example, but its explanatory status remains disputed. The entry concludes that the debate is unresolved and that rejecting indispensability does not by itself prove nominalism.
key_ideas: The argument can be stated as: scientific ontology should include indispensable entities; mathematics is indispensable to our best science; therefore mathematical entities should be included.
Indispensability is not simply eliminability. A replacement must remain scientifically attractive, considering virtues such as empirical success, simplicity, unification, and explanatory power.
Naturalism supports looking to science when deciding what exists, while confirmational holism is meant to support commitment to all components of a confirmed theory.
Field challenges the second premise by arguing that mathematics may be conservative and pragmatically useful, while scientific theories may be nominalized at least in important cases.

Maddy and Sober challenge the relation between naturalism and holism, noting that scientists may distinguish among the commitments of a theory and that mathematics may not receive empirical confirmation in the same way.
Explanatory versions shift attention from mathematics being used everywhere to mathematics making a genuine difference to a scientific explanation.
summaries.why_it_matters: The argument connects abstract mathematics with concrete scientific success. It raises a general philosophical question: when a theory works, which of its claims are we entitled to believe? It also clarifies differences between realism, nominalism, scientific evidence, and explanation. Even if mathematics is indispensable in practice, that alone may not settle whether mathematical entities exist or what kind of support mathematical theories receive.

important_terms.definition: A claim that we should accept the existence of every entity, and only those entities, that is indispensable to our best scientific theories.
A view that philosophy is continuous with science and that our best scientific theories guide judgments about what exists.
The position that mathematical entities, such as numbers or sets, exist independently of human thought or language.
A position that seeks to avoid commitment to abstract mathematical entities while still accounting for mathematical language and practice.
The thesis that empirical evidence supports a theory as a whole rather than separately confirming each component.
A theory or entity is dispensable when it can be removed and replaced by an attractive alternative that preserves the relevant scientific virtues.
A form of the argument claiming that mathematics is indispensable because it contributes to scientific explanations, not merely to calculation or convenient formulation.
A proposed reformulation of a scientific theory that removes quantification over mathematical entities.

questions_to_think_about: If a mathematical assumption helps produce a successful prediction, does that support the truth of the assumption itself?
What should count as an attractive replacement for a theory that removes mathematical entities?
Can a theory be confirmed as a whole if scientists reasonably reject some of its idealizations or components?
Does the cicada example show that mathematics explains a biological fact, or only that biology can be described mathematically?
If the indispensability argument fails, does that establish nominalism, or merely remove one argument for realism?

summaries.example: Suppose a school models the spread of a rumor with a graph and an equation. The equation helps predict how many students may hear the rumor next. One philosopher might say that because the equation is essential to the best model, the mathematical structure should count as part of what the model says is real. Another might answer that the equation is a convenient way to describe relationships among actual students. Its usefulness does not automatically prove that numbers or functions exist as independent things.
summaries.summary: Mathematics is used throughout science: it helps express theories, calculate consequences, make predictions, and sometimes provide explanations. The Quine-Putnam indispensability argument treats this role as evidence about reality. It proposes that we should be committed to the entities required by our best scientific theories, and that mathematical entities are among those requirements. Therefore, it concludes, numbers, sets, functions, and similar entities exist. This position is a form of mathematical realism or platonism. Nominalists seek ways to describe science without commitment to such abstract objects. A central issue is what “indispensable” means. It cannot mean merely that a mathematical formulation cannot be translated into any other formulation, since a theory may be replaced in a less attractive form. Instead, the replacement must preserve scientific virtues such as simplicity, empirical success, unification, and explanatory power. Naturalism gives the argument its science-centered approach to ontology. Confirmational holism is intended to support the idea that when evidence confirms a scientific theory, it also supports the mathematics used within it. Critics dispute this. Field argues that mathematics may be conservative and pragmatically useful rather than ontologically necessary. Maddy emphasizes tensions between holism and scientific and mathematical practice, while Sober questions whether mathematics is empirically confirmed like competing scientific hypotheses. Explanatory versions offer a different route: mathematics might support realism if it makes a genuine explanatory contribution. The entry reports that these disputes remain active and that defeating the argument would not automatically establish nominalism.
key_ideas: The argument associated with Quine and Putnam begins with mathematics’ widespread role in science and concludes that mathematical entities should be included in our picture of reality.
Its first premise says that our best scientific theories should determine which entities we are committed to. Its second says that mathematics cannot be left out of those theories.
The meaning of “indispensable” is controversial: a theory might be replaceable in principle but still be preferable because it is simpler, more unified, or more explanatory.
Naturalism supports science as a guide to existence, while confirmational holism is used to explain why the mathematics in a confirmed theory should receive support too.
Field argues that mathematics may be useful without being indispensable in the stronger sense, because it can simplify reasoning while remaining conservative about physical claims.
Explanatory versions ask whether mathematics helps explain scientific phenomena, rather than merely representing them efficiently.
summaries.why_it_matters: The topic tests how far scientific success reaches into metaphysics. A theory may use an idea constantly without settling whether that idea names something real. The debate also separates several questions that are often mixed together: whether mathematics is useful, whether it is necessary, whether it is true, and whether it explains. These distinctions are important for understanding both mathematics and science.

important_terms.definition: So necessary for a successful purpose that removing it would leave no comparably good theory or method.
A philosophical account of what exists or what we should say exists.
The view that mathematical objects are real, even though they are not ordinary physical objects.
The view that mathematics can be understood without commitment to abstract mathematical objects.
The idea that science and philosophy should look to successful scientific methods when deciding what exists.
The claim that evidence often supports a whole theory, rather than separately supporting every sentence or part of it.
A reformulation of a scientific theory that removes references to mathematical objects.

questions_to_think_about: Does a model’s usefulness show that its mathematical parts are true?
Should scientists’ different attitudes toward different parts of a theory affect philosophical conclusions about what exists?
What makes a replacement theory attractive enough to show that mathematics is dispensable?
Is a mathematical pattern part of an explanation, or just a helpful description?
If one argument for realism is weakened, what other conclusions remain open?
